content.section: ACS management in patients with cancer
content.summary: Diagnosis and management of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients with cancer follow the same principles as in patients without cancer but are complicated by frailty, increased bleeding risk, thrombocytopaenia, and increased thrombotic risk. Temporary interruption of cancer treatment and an urgent multidisciplinary approach are recommended. Invasive management (including PCI with DES) is recommended for ACS patients with cancer if prognosis is >6 months or if the patient is unstable. For advanced cancer or life expectancy <6 months, a conservative strategy may be considered. When coronary anatomy is not amenable to PCI, CABG can be considered after multidisciplinary discussion if cancer prognosis is >12 months. Given high bleeding risk (HBR), the preferred P2Y12 inhibitor for ACS patients with active cancer is clopidogrel. Potential drug–drug interactions with cancer therapies should be checked when using ticagrelor or clopidogrel because pharmacokinetic interactions via CYP450 may occur. If acute ischaemia is provoked by cancer therapy, alternative cancer therapies should be considered after multidisciplinary discussion; cancer drugs associated with thrombosis or MI should be stopped and reviewed. Non–MI-associated cancer therapies can be restarted after revascularization when indicated and the patient is stabilized on ACS medical therapy. Supplementary data and 2022 ESC Guidelines on cardio-oncology are referenced. A separate section addresses COVID-19 impact on ACS management.
key_points: Active cancer diagnosed in the past 12 months is considered HBR per ARC-HBR criteria.
Invasive management is recommended for ACS in cancer patients if prognosis >6 months or patient unstable; conservative strategy may be used for advanced cancer with life expectancy <6 months.
Preferred P2Y12 inhibitor for ACS patients with active cancer is clopidogrel (due to HBR considerations).
Check for drug–drug interactions between antiplatelets (ticagrelor, clopidogrel) and cancer therapies (possible CYP450-mediated interactions).
Review and stop cancer drugs associated with thrombosis or MI after ACS; restart non-associated therapies after stabilization and when revascularization is complete if indicated.
content.notes: Page mentions P2Y12 inhibitor preference and warns about CYP450-mediated drug interactions but does not specify individual CYP genes.
